LOCAL HISTORY
Before the Kestrel Diner, there was Whitlow's Garage
As the city moves to redevelop the Fourth Street site, the building that became the Kestrel Diner stands as one of the last visible remnants of its early motoring trade.

by Ellen Farriday
May 5, 2026
 
In this undated (but, likely, 1930s) photo, the Whitlow's sign reads, "Tyres, petrol and a fair price." Courtesy of the County Library for Local History

In the early 1950s, when the suburbs spread outward and every second household kept a car, filling stations and roadside cafes appeared along the county roads almost overnight. Fourth Street was no exception, and the garages came with them.

Whitlow's and the others from that decade are long gone, but two buildings from an earlier era are still recognisable today. Of the two, the Kestrel Diner on Fourth Street is slated for demolition.

By 1931, the owners had remodelled the building into a lunch counter with an enclosed circular bar, which the local paper described at the time as almost aggressively modern.

In 1931, Whitlow's Garage advertised in the "County Almanac," a local trade publication. Courtesy of the County Almanac

In 1940, the counter was pulled out and replaced with a new building and a new name, and the garage trade moved two streets east where the road was wider and the turning easier.

Whitlow's Garage on Fourth Street, in 1955. Courtesy of Robert Whitlow
